[?1] Tissues in plants

[?] A group of cells with similar structure makes tissues and [?forms] the same task. There are three types of tissues in [?nts] on the basis of their functions i.e. dermal tissues, [?und] tissues and vascular tissues.
[?] Dermal Tissue

[?] Dermal tissues form the protective covering of the plant organs. They [?] present at periphery of root, stem and leaves. The cells of the dermal [?ues] are epidermal cells, stomata and trichomes. In leaves, they control [?] gaseous exchange through stomata. In stem and roots, epidermal cells [?end] into trichomes. Trichomes are very thin and small hair like extensions [?bsorb] more water (roots) and protect the plants against herbivores. The [?mal] tissues in leaves and stems are protected by waxy cuticle.

The cells of ground tissues are made [?] of parenchyma cells, collenchyma cells and sclerenchyma cells. [?enchyma] cells are photosynthetic in leaves while store food in the roots. [?llenchyma] cells support the shoot when there is active growth, [?erenchyma] cells support the shoot in the areas where growth has ceased.

1.2 Plant Organs and their Structures
Roots, stem and leaves are major plant organs.
i. Roots
The structure and arrangement of tissues in roots facilitate the functions of the root i.e. hold the plant firmly in soil and absorb water and nutrients from the soil and conduct it to the stem.
Fig. 1.3 Branch system of roots
External structure
In dicot plants, the root that arises from radical is called primary or [ta?]

[?oot]. The subsequent branches of tap root [?re] called secondary roots and so on. [?ach] root has root hair and root cap. In [?onocot] plants, roots arise from the stem [?aterally] or from the hypocotyl. They are [?alled] fibrous roots.
Fig. 1.4 (a) Taproot, (b) Fibrous [root?]
[?nternal] structure of root
Root being an organ has specific [?rrangement] of different tissues in [?ubsequent] layers. These are discussed below:
[?] Epidermis: It is the outermost protective layer. The cells have [no?] [?ntercellular] spaces. It gives rise to root hair.
[?] Cortex: Cortex is a region that contains multiple layers of cells that [?onduct] water from epidermis to the inner layers of cells.
[?] Endodermis: Next to cortex, single or two layers of cells known as [?ndodermis]. Their cells lack intra-cellular spaces. It controls water transport. [?] surrounds central region known as stele.
[?] Pericycle/cambium: The single layer of cells next to endodermis is [?alled] pericycle. It develops lateral roots and provides support to vascular [?issues].

[?] Vascular bundle: Vascular bundle (xylem and phloem) are located [?ntrally] to withstand stretching forces and conduct water and food [?spectively].
[?] Pith: Pith is the central region in roots. In dicots, it is less prominent or [?most] absent. Its cells have large intercellular spaces and store food.

iii. Leaves
Leaves are the food factories. Their structures facilitate them in making food.
Internal structure of a leaf

The internal structure of a leaf has three distinct layers of cells such as epidermis, mesophyll, and vascular bundles. The epidermis is the uppermost and the lowermost layer of a leaf. It is protected by a waxy layer called the cuticle. The lower epidermis contains stomata (special openings for gaseous exchange) surrounded by two guard cells.

The layer below the epidermis is of mesophyll. The mesophyll is ground tissue that consists of two types of parenchymatous cells such [?] palisade mesophyll cells and spongy mesophyll cells. Palisade [mesoph?] cells are columnar and lie exactly below the epidermis. They have [?]

[?intercellular spaces among them. Spongy mesophyll cells lie below ?] palisade mesophylls cells. They have intercellular spaces and [irregu?] shapes. Due to the intercellular spaces, they have been named ['Spon?] cells. Among the spongy mesophyll cells, vascular bundles are found. 1.3 Organ Systems in Plants
A plant has two major organ systems: root system and shoot system.

The root system anchors plants into the soil; absorbs nutrients and water from the soil. Moreover, it provides a shelter to nitrogen-fixing bacteria to provide nitrogen to plants. The [sho?] system produces fruit and seeds, which transfer their characteristics [?] features to new plants. Moreover, it prepares food for whole of the [pl?] through photosynthesis.
The shoot system grows positively towards light while root [syst?] grows positively towards gravity. The internal structures of [org?]
[?] both systems facilitate the energy and food production processes i.e. [?pirations] and photosynthesis respectively.
[BOX Fig. 1.9 label] [?] Shoot system: Grows above [?] ground. Its organs are stem, [?ves], flowers, fruit and nodes.
[BOX Fig. 1.9 label] [?] Root system: Lies below the [?und]. Its organs are primary root [?d] its branches i.e. secondary, [?tiary], quaternary roots and root [?irs].

B. Systems and Processes in Plants

There are many processes taking place in plants. These [?] necessary to keep plants alive. The major systems are [?nsportation] system, food and energy production systems. [?re] we will study these systems in detail.
[?4] Transport System in Plants
Transport system in plants serves the two purposes: i.e.
It absorbs and transports water and minerals. It is called transpiration.
It distributes food from leaves to all other parts. It is called translocation.
[?4.1] Transpiration (Movement of water)

Transpiration is the loss of water from the aerial parts of the plants such [?] leaves and stems. As a result, new water is absorbed from the soil by the [?ots]. It creates a pressure difference between the root (high pressure due to

[?top line cut: ... (low pressure due to the release ... ?] water) causing more absorption of water through the roots. [T?] phenomenon takes place against gravity. The upward movement of [wate?] the xylem vessels is called transpiration stream.
Two factors or properties promote the transpiration stream:
i. Cohesion: Due to forces of attraction, water molecules join [togeth?] and drag themselves up in the xylem column.

ii. Adhesion: the force of attraction between xylem walls and [wa?] molecules cause capillary action and drag water upward in the [xyl?] vessels. These two factors along with suction pressure (due to transpiration) develop a continuous column of water in the xylem vessel. As a result, water moves upward and reaches the uppermost parts of the plants.

[?ctors] Affecting Transpiration in Plants
Rate of transpiration is affected by the following [?vironmental] factors.

[?] Humidity: Water vapours present in the air affect the rate of transpiration. The rate of transpiration is inversely proportional to the humidity. Rate of transpiration decreases with increase of humidity in the air.
[?] Temperature: Increase in temperature decreases the humidity and opens the stomata. As a result, rate of transpiration increases.
[?] Light Intensity: Light increases the rate of transpiration by opening the stomata.
[?] Air/Wind speed: Rate of transpiration increases with wind speed because the saturated air around the leaves is removed.

1.5 Food making in plants – Photosynthesis

As you know, plants prepare their food themselves. Food making is a multi-step process. It takes place in leaves mainly, where chloroplast is present. The chloroplast contains a green pigment called chlorophyll. It traps heat and light from the sun rays falling over it. Carbon dioxide (air) enters into the leaf cells through stomata and the xylem cells provide water.

In the presence of sunlight, and chlorophyl carbon dioxide and [wat?] react and make glucose and oxygen. Glucose is the food of plants. [Oxygen?] a by-product of this reaction and is released from the plants [throu?] stomata. The whole process is called photosynthesis. It is defined as ["t?] process by which green plants transform light energy into chemical [ener?] using carbon dioxide and water." The process is summarized in the [giv?] word equation:
Carbon dioxide + water —(Light / Chlorophyll)→ glucose + oxygen.
Light is written above the arrow because it does not take part in [t?] reaction. It just triggers the reaction.
Adaptations of Leaves for Photosynthesis
Leaves are the food factories. Their structure is adapted [f?] photosynthesis, such as:
i. The broad shape of leaves provide large surface area that receives maximum sunlight.
ii. Due to the thin leaf-width, carbon dioxide quickly diffuses into the mesophyll cells.
iii. Inside the leaf, chlorophyll is arranged in thylakoid stacks for receiving maximum energy from sunlight.

[BOX Interesting information] If photosynthesis would stop, [the?] there would be a very few [survivi?] organisms on the Earth because it [?] the only known mechanism [throu?] which inorganic [compoun?] (carbon dioxide and water) turn [?] to organic compound.
[?iv.] [?top line cut: The closely packed arrangement of palisade mesophyll cells prevent an?] loss of diffused carbon dioxide and light energy.

[?v.] For gaseous exchange, stomata are present. Each stoma surrounds [b?] two guard cells. Their opening and closing mechanism regulates the [flo?] of carbon dioxide and maintains the balance of water in the cells. [I?] other words, stomata keep a check on water loss and intake of [carbo?] dioxide
[?vi.] The large intercellular spaces among spongy mesophyll cells, [allo?] gaseous exchange.
[?vii.] Thick waxy cuticle above epidermis prevents excess loss of [wate?] through evaporation.
[?viii.] Plants growing in sunny environment have high rate of [photosynthesis?] Therefore, such plants have more thick layers of palisade [mesophyll?] cells.

[?1.6] Energy Production in Plants (Cellular Respiration)

Cellular respiration is the production of energy from the [?lucose] produced during photosynthesis. In plants, the food [?olecules] (glucose) enter into the phloem vessels and reach all the [?ells] of the plants. The oxygen produced in photosynthesis or [?aking] from air reaches the cells and takes part in the process of [?ellular] respiration.
The process of cellular respiration begins in the cytoplasm, produces 2 ATP [?olecules] and 2 molecules of pyruvic acid from 1 molecule of glucose. [?his] process is called glycolysis.
Glucose → 2 Pyruvic acid + 2 ATD.
In absence of oxygen, pyruvic acid breaks down into lactic acid and produces 2 ATP molecules. It is an anaerobic respiration.
2 Pyruvic acid → Lactic acid + + 2 ATP.

In the presence of oxygen, this pyruvic acid enters into [mitochondri?] for the second phase of aerobic respiration called Krebs cycle; it involves [?] series of the chemical reactions and releases energy in the form of [34-?] ATP molecules.
Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + [34-36 A?]
1.7 Comparison Between Photosynthesis and [Respirati?]

Photosynthesis and respiration are complementary processes to each other. They maintain the oxygen-carbon dioxide balance in nature together. However, they are different from one another. Some of the major differences between them are mentioned below:

1.8 Minerals required by plants

Plants need minerals along with carbon dioxide and water to [surviv?] They need mineral elements for normal and healthy growth. Plants [u?] minerals to make food molecules such as protein out of the glucose [durin?] photosynthesis.
1.8.1 How minerals get into plants?

Mineral elements from the soil enter the roots of plants in the form of solution. Some of the minerals dissolved in the water enter the root hair cells. However, most minerals are moved into the plant root cells using energy. This is because there are usually fewer minerals in the soil than in the plant cells. Energy [?] needed to pull minerals into the root cells.
[?ole] of Magnesium in plant Growth

Magnesium is required by the plant cells to capture energy needed [fo?] [?hotosynthesis]. Without magnesium chlorophyll cannot capture the [Su?] [?nergy]. Magnesium is essential to make chlorphyll which gives green [colou?] [?o] leaves.
[?ole] of Nitrates in plant Growth

Nitrates are nitrogen based compounds. Plants absorb nitrates from [th?] [?oil] and utilize them to make proteins. Farmers also use fertilizers [containin?] [?itrates] to increase the yield and growth of crops.
Key Points
The root system includes those parts of the plant that present below the ground in soil.
Shoot system includes those parts of the plants that are present above the ground.
Xylem cells are known as water conducting cells. Phloem cells transport food produced by the leaves throughout the plant (translocation).
Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants and some other organisms use sunlight to synthesize nutrients from carbon dioxide and water.
Respiration is a process in living organisms involving the production of energy, typically with the intake of oxygen and release of carbon dioxide from the oxidation of complex organic substances.
Different factors like temperature, humidity, wind speed and light intensity affect the rate of transpiration.
Aerobic respiration requires oxygen while anaerobic respiration does not require oxygen.
Magnesium is used by chlorophyll to capture energy and nitrates are used by plants to produce protein.
